title: Anger, the burning thief
hook: krodh burns the one who holds it; righteous anger is guided by compassion

segments.voice: Yesterday, truth: high, and higher still, truthful living. Your line was truth in conduct. Did you keep the small promise, at the time you picked? Day one thousand four hundred.

A coal, picked up bare-handed to throw at someone. Before it ever reaches them, whose hand is already burning? It's a simple picture. The Guru Granth Sahib names anger, krodh, among five thieves living inside the body. This one doesn't break in. It flares up from inside, and the first thing it burns is the one holding it. Yet the Gurus also spoke fiercely against cruelty. So which is it? Today: anger, and what to do in the second before it.
screen: `A COAL IN A BARE HAND.` → `KRODH, THE BURNING THIEF.` → `ANGER.`

segments.voice: First, Guru Arjan speaks to anger directly. In one of his saloks in the Granth he addresses it like a person. In paraphrase: O anger, root of strife, compassion never rises in you. Then, the saloks go on, it takes people over and makes them dance to its tune. That's the thief at work. It doesn't just add heat. It pushes compassion out of the room. Remember the Japji's bull a few days ago: dharma is the son of compassion. Anger shoves the mother out of her chair. Second, Farid's answer. In one of his couplets, in paraphrase: Farid, answer evil with good; don't fill your mind with anger. Then your body won't fall sick, and you'll gain everything. Notice the body. Farid knows anger lives in the chest and the jaw and the stomach, and that it wears the holder down first. Third, the other anger. The Gurus were not quiet in the face of wrong. Guru Nanak cried out against the cruelty of an invading army; we heard that protest days ago. So there is a fierce response to injustice in this tradition. The difference is what steers it. Krodh is anger for me: my pride hurt, my plan blocked. The fierceness the Gurus show is for others, and it's guided by compassion, not by the thief. Fourth, the gap. Anger is fast. The way the tradition slows it down is remembering, Simran, and in plain terms, a breath. One breath before the word. One breath before the send button. In that gap, compassion gets a chance to come back into the chair. Back to the coal: one breath can be long enough to notice it's in your own hand, and set it down.
screen: `ARJAN: ANGER, ROOT OF STRIFE.` · `FARID: ANSWER EVIL WITH GOOD.` · `FIERCE FOR OTHERS, GUIDED BY COMPASSION.` · `ONE BREATH BEFORE THE WORD.` · then, large: `BREATHE FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: breathe before anger. Settle. Bring to mind one small thing that reliably irritates you. A slow driver. A certain tone in a certain voice. A dish left in the sink. Let a little of the heat come, just a little. Now notice where it lands in your body: jaw, chest, hands. Then take one slow breath, all the way in and all the way out, before you think a single word about it. Do that again. And again. Watch what the heat does when it's given breaths instead of words. The bell holds the time.
Anger. Krodh, one of the five thieves: it burns the one who holds it and pushes compassion out; the fierceness the Gurus honor is guided by compassion. Today's word.
Your line: breathe first. Today, the next time you feel the heat rise, take one full breath before you speak or type. Just one. Then decide. Day one thousand four hundred.

howItsDone: Sikhs name krodh, anger, among the five thieves, kaam, krodh, lobh, moh and ahankar, and meet them through Naam Simran, the remembrance of the Lord, and the company of the sangat.

original.note: Gurmukhi: krodh, anger, one of the five thieves the Granth names.

trapdoor: what you thought: religion says never get angry.
what it means: krodh, anger for the self, burns the holder and drives out compassion; fierceness for others must be steered by compassion.
what a scholar hears: Guru Arjan's salok addresses anger as root of strife, and Farid's couplet says answer evil with good.

notes: Please confirm Ang 1358 for the Sahaskriti salok addressed to anger and that 'makes them dance to its tune' fairly paraphrases its continuation (recalled as making people dance like monkeys).
Please confirm the Ang (1381 or 1382) for Farid's 'buraa de bhalaa kar' couplet and the paraphrase.
The 'burning thief' is the outline title's image; no specific Granth line about anger burning is quoted.
The reference back to Guru Nanak's protest (Babarvani, taught day 1385) is brief and paraphrased.

Editor: removed the recall of a Kabir 'anger is death' couplet (day 1397 no longer uses it; the Granth's Ang 1372 salok pairs greed, not anger, with death) and recalled the Japji's bull instead; cut the week look-back (days 1386 and 1393 used the device) for a close on the hook's coal; reworded the hook's line about 'the title'. 'One breath can be long enough' is the script's own encouragement, not a text claim.
